item.title: The food bank helping pet owners with rising bills
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth reporting on a social issue with clear context and vocabulary

The food bank helping pet owners with rising bills

At Burngreave Foodbank in Sheffield, a queue of worried people are here not to collect groceries for themselves, but food for their pets.

The RSPCA has launched a pop-up food bank to hand out cat litter, veterinary vouchers and pet toys as well as food.

Many of the dog and cat owners using the service say that rising bills are leaving them in fear they will not be able to care for their beloved companions.

John Paul Feely, 59, has four cats and a dog, and currently spends Â£35 a month on them.

"At the moment we're facing rises in fuel costs, food costs and you've got to make a choice at some point, can we look after the animals?" he says.

Feely worries that unexpected vet bills as well as the day-to-day expenses could tip him over the edge when his energy bill goes up in January.

Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.

A typical bill will increase by about Â£37 a month in the first three months of the new year.

The government will pay millions of households Â£100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.

Feely lives with his partner and explains that they are already making tough decisions about "turning the lights out and not putting the heating on".

He is able to take home food supplies and a dog chew toy.

As food bank volunteers offer tea and coffee to those waiting in the queue, Angela Gillot accepts a small dog jacket from the RSPCA stall with a smile.

She explains with a tear in her eye that since becoming unemployed she has felt the pinch of rising bills.

The RSPCA estimates that the cost of keeping a small dog like a Jack Russell could be up to Â£209 a month.

Energy costs going up next year "will affect everything," Gillot admits, as she describes how she and her dog huddle up under a blanket to keep warm.

"We do love these pets. We're a pet-loving nation aren't we? But it's getting harder.

"When I got my dogs I was working, so I try my best, but the price of food, especially what's of quality, I just really can't afford it.

"It's not often you go to these places and they think about your pets," the 58-year-old says.

Tricia Watts, the upbeat assistant manger at Burngreave Foodbank, is enthusiastic about the support from the RSPCA.

She explains that while the food bank works with people in food poverty, it cannot always help people with animal care as it relies on donations.

She has seen demand increase, and donations fall, in the seven years she has worked at the food bank.

"I think pets are so important to people. If people are going through hard times, they're still important and they don't want to lose them."

Growing bills are of particular concern to exotic animal owners as many birds, reptiles and fish must be kept in carefully maintained conditions that are often energy-intensive.

Carl Chandler runs Sustainable Aquatics in Rotherham. He says rising energy prices have had a "gigantic" impact on his business.

Chandler caveats that fish are one of the most wallet-friendly pets.

"To run a tropical fish tank you're looking less than a cup of coffee a week."

Other species, however, require specialist equipment to replicate their natural habitats.

"Reptiles, frogs and amphibians are incredibly expensive to heat because you need UV bulbs and to keep the right humidity."

Back in Burngreave, the pop-up event has managed to give away as much as 50kg of food, the equivalent of more than 100 tins, to pet owners in need.

Sometimes, of course, owners find the challenge simply too much, and give their pets up for rehoming.

"We've seen heartbreaking examples across the country of people leaving notes with animals saying they just can't afford them any more," Chris O'Brien, a spokesperson for the RSPCA, says.

"The cost of giving crisis has put new levels of pressure on us in terms of animals coming in quicker than we can rehome them.

"As these cost of living bombshells keep coming, unfortunately it's going to be a continued difficult time for animal owners across the region."

item.title: Sephora’s U.S. CEO initially turned down an entry-level job at the company because she could only wear black, white, or gray to the office
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Engaging narrative with business leadership insight and cultural context

In 1998, Artemis Patrick turned down a job at a relatively small perfume brand that had just been acquired by the luxury giant LVMH. That company was Sephora, and 26 years later, she became its North America CEO.

Patrick stepped into the top job for the global beauty retailer’s North America division in April 2024, earning a shoutout in its parent company’s half-year earnings call in July for “good performance.”

But Patrick’s journey to the top of the cosmetics empire started with a detour into cigarettes.

Patrick was studying for her MBA at San Francisco State University when a friend introduced her to the LVMH brand, which was hiring for entry-level planning roles. Patrick initially went in to interview for a role at the duty-free giant DFS in the only category that was hiring: tobacco.

“I thought, oh my gosh, what am I going to be peddling cigarettes?” Patrick told the “How Leaders Lead” podcast in a recent episode. “This is crazy. So I [asked] if they had anything else, and she said, well there is this company called Sephora—LVMH just acquired it—and it sells fragrance.”

“Same salary, same building, because at the time Sephora was sharing the office floor with DFS. And I said, I mean, obviously I’ll take the beauty job. She said there’s only one catch: You have to wear black white, or gray.”

“And I said, I’ll take the cigarette job.”

Patrick, who emigrated to the U.S. from Iran at the age of 7, said her decision to take the DFS role rather than the beauty job wasn’t necessarily down to independence but rather to personal finances. After all, Patrick was a student, and her wardrobe was full of patterned dresses—she couldn’t afford to repurchase multiple monochromatic looks.

DFS turned out to be an “incredible opportunity” that took Patrick around the world and quickly propelled her from the cigarette category into wine. But in 2006, Sephora came calling again courtesy of a referral from Carolyn Bojanowski, now Sephora’s executive vice president for merchandising.

Patrick interviewed with the same HR representative she had turned down years before, and the corporate dress code of black, white, and gray (“concept colors,” as they were referred to at the time) was still in place.

“They’d added red to the concept at that point,” Patrick recalls. “It was actually another, I think, six or seven years before we added color.”

Building diverse teams

Patrick’s path to Sephora and then up its ranks wasn’t linear—after DFS she worked at Restoration Hardware and Peet’s Coffee & Tea—and said this diversity of experience is now precisely what she looks for when building her own teams.

“I feel that my job is to remove obstacles and to make sure that they get to do what we hired them to do,” added Patrick. “So I definitely believe in building diverse teams, and I do feel that my job as a leader is to protect them from the noise and deal with the things that I should be dealing with.”

item.title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed explanation of a complex business deal with clear prose

UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals

The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.

The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.

It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.

Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.

Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

Fee details

According to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.

The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.

This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.

But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.

The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.

However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.

Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer".

'Extraordinary powers'

It comes as the government published separate legislation granting it broad powers to incorporate new EU laws required to implement the agreements, without having to hold a full vote each time.

The food standards deal in particular will mean Britain will have to align with scores of current EU food-related laws that have been updated since Brexit, along with future rules in these areas.

The government argues the new powers are required because it would be impractical to run a full parliamentary process each time UK legislation needs to be updated to make the agreement work.

But it has prompted criticism from opposition parties, because the UK no longer has voting rights at the EU to shape European legislation.

The government argues the UK will get a say on new rules, with the treaty texts confirming British experts can be consulted when new EU laws are being drawn up, with the UK granted "observer" status in certain meetings.

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was showing "disdain for the democratic process" by asking for a "blank cheque to install and enact EU law".

"The prime minister is telling MPs to hand him extraordinary powers whilst having no idea what the EU will actually agree to," she added.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued the Burnham's deals would take Britain back into "much of the European Union's single market".

He added: "European economies are not growing as fast as ours. The idea that getting closer to the EU will mean growth for us is a myth."

Source: BBC Business | Published: 2026-11-26 23:17 UTC | Difficulty: 70/100

item.title: I spend £200 a month on fancy meals by myself - would you dine solo?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Interesting trend piece with personal anecdotes and industry analysis

My self-care is booking a table at a fancy restaurant - on my own

Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosÃ©, she looks across at the empty seat opposite - bliss.

"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.

The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.

As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."

We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.

Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.

She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending Â£100 to Â£200 per meal.

"I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says.

"I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."

Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering".

"It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."

Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category.

Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.

Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi.

"Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast.

"It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."

A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media.

"Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.

Ruth Alexander hears from solo diners - some who find peace and joy in a table for one, and others who would much rather not be alone

Banks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational".

But he notes that not every restaurant has welcomed the trend.

"A single diner could therefore feel like an inefficient use of a table rather than a customer the restaurant actively wanted."

SoloTable, a website that helps identify restaurants suitable for solo diners, found that one in eight of 178 restaurants it surveyed in London did not accept online reservations from solo diners.

Catherine says she has previously been turned away. "There are a lot of restaurants that I've wanted to go to before where they don't actually allow solo diners. And I've always found that to be really disappointing."

However, some restaurants like Jungli, an Indian restaurant in Newcastle upon Tyne, is working to attract solo diners.

Co-founder and director Yousaf Khalid has included high tables and bar seats in his recently opened restaurant. They also have charging points for laptops and phones.

"We want people to feel comfortable in these sorts of environments, being able to walk in on their own," he says.

He has hired staff with "bigger personalities" to engage customers in conversation but they also know when to leave diners alone if they want a more solitary experience.

Catherine urges anyone who fancies solo dining to give it a go.

"Food is a great way to bring people together, but it's also a great way to have good experiences on your own.

"I think with time, people will see and will start to accept it as something that's more normal."

Additional reporting by Jemma Crew and Emma Jackson.
